title.en: ExceptionGroup and except*: Reporting Many Failures At Once

description.en: Python 3.11 can raise several errors as one ExceptionGroup, and catch them by type with except*. Learn to collect every failure in a batch instead of stopping at the first.

story_variants.en:
## One Failure Is Not The Whole Story

"A normal `raise` carries exactly one exception," Vaathiyaar says. "But real programs run many things at once -- a batch of files, a dozen network calls -- and several can fail in the same run. If you raise only the first failure you hide the other eleven. Python 3.11 added **`ExceptionGroup`**: one exception that carries a list of others."

### Build A Group

```python
errors = [ValueError("empty"), ValueError("bad number")]
raise ExceptionGroup("batch failed", errors)
```

The first argument is a message; the second is a **non-empty** list of exceptions. Passing an empty list, or something that is not an exception, raises `ValueError`. Printing the group shows `batch failed (2 sub-exceptions)`, and `group.exceptions` is the tuple of members.

### Catch By Type With `except*`

An ordinary `except ValueError` asks "is this exception a ValueError?" -- but a group is an `ExceptionGroup`, not a `ValueError`. So 3.11 added **`except*`**, which asks "does this group *contain* any ValueErrors?" The clause receives a *new group holding only the matching members*:

```python
try:
    run_all(["1", "", "x", None])
except* ValueError as group:
    print(len(group.exceptions))   # 2
except* TypeError as group:
    print(len(group.exceptions))   # 1
```

Unlike plain `except`, **every** `except*` clause that matches something runs, each with its own slice of the group. Anything no clause handled is re-raised afterwards as a smaller group, so nothing is silently lost.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** you cannot mix `except` and `except*` in one `try`, and `return`, `break` and `continue` are not allowed inside an `except*` block (both are `SyntaxError`s). Also, `except*` works on a plain exception too: it wraps it in a one-member group so your handler code stays the same.

Today you write the collector that builds a group, then the handler that splits it with `except*`.

explanation.en: Keep each failure instead of stopping at the first one
Raise all collected failures together as one exception

instruction.en: Implement `run_all(items)`: call `parse` on every item, keep going after a failure, and collect the exceptions. If any failed, raise `ExceptionGroup("batch failed", errors)`; otherwise return the list of parsed numbers. Then print `run_all(["1", "2"])` (expected: `[1, 2]`).

en: Wrap parse(item) in try/except Exception as exc and append exc to errors
After the loop, if errors: raise ExceptionGroup("batch failed", errors)

instruction.en: Now implement `summarize(items)` using `except*`: call `run_all(items)` and return `(number of ValueErrors, number of TypeErrors)` that it reported. Use `len(group.exceptions)` inside each clause. Then print `summarize(["1", "", "x", None, "5"])` (expected: `(2, 1)`).

en: Use two clauses: except* ValueError as group and except* TypeError as group
Inside each, set the count to len(group.exceptions)
Do not use plain except here: it cannot see inside an ExceptionGroup

practice_challenges.test_code:
assert summarize(["1", "", "x", None, "5"]) == (2, 1), f"got {summarize(['1', '', 'x', None, '5'])}"
assert summarize(["1", "2"]) == (0, 0), "no failures should give (0, 0)"
assert summarize([None, None, None]) == (0, 3), "three TypeErrors"

under_the_hood.summary: An ExceptionGroup is an ordinary exception object that holds a tuple of other exceptions; except* walks that tree, hands each matching clause a new group of the matching leaves, and re-raises whatever nobody claimed.

steps.title: A group is an exception that holds exceptions
steps.body: `ExceptionGroup(msg, excs)` stores the message and a tuple of members in `.exceptions`. The list must be non-empty and every item must be an exception, otherwise the constructor raises `ValueError`. Members can themselves be groups, so a group is really a tree.

left.label: Plain raise
left.code:
raise ValueError('empty')
# one exception, one traceback

right.label: Group
right.code:
raise ExceptionGroup('batch failed', [
    ValueError('empty'),
    TypeError('None'),
])
# one exception carrying two

steps.title: Why plain except cannot see inside
steps.body: `except ValueError` tests `isinstance(exc, ValueError)`. The group is an `ExceptionGroup`, which is not a `ValueError`, so the clause would not match even though a ValueError is inside. `except*` was added to look inside the group instead.

steps.title: except* gives each clause a new group
steps.body: For each `except*` clause, Python picks the leaves that match its type and builds a new group of them (same message, same nesting). The clause body runs with that group bound to the `as` name. Clauses are tried in order, and a leaf is claimed by the first clause that matches it.

stepDescriptions.description: A group with three leaves is raised.
Leaves that are ValueErrors (1 and 3) are gathered into a new group.
Leaves that remain (the TypeError) go to the next clause, which prints 1.

steps.title: Leftovers are re-raised
steps.body: If some leaves match no clause, Python raises them again as a new group once the handlers finish, so an unexpected KeyError cannot vanish. If every leaf was handled, execution simply continues after the try statement.

steps.title: Why the restrictions exist
steps.body: Several handlers can run for one raise, so a `return`, `break` or `continue` inside one would decide what happens to the others. Python forbids them in `except*` blocks, and also forbids mixing `except` with `except*` in the same `try`. Both are SyntaxErrors.

under_the_hood.takeaway: A group is a tree of exceptions. Catch by type with except*, which splits the tree, and remember that anything unhandled comes back out instead of disappearing.
